title: For one another
hook: nature made us for one another, so wronging others wrongs the whole (Meditations 9.1)
tomorrow: Death as a work of nature

segments.voice: Yesterday: teach or bear with them, and no third door. Your line was teach or bear. Which door did you choose, and with whom? Day six hundred six.

A cashier gives you too much change. Ten dollars, maybe. Nobody saw. The store is big; it'll never notice. There may be a small tug anyway, even if it's hard to say why. Book nine of the Meditations opens with Marcus's answer, and it's bigger than ten dollars. He says a wrong like that isn't only against the cashier. It's against the whole. Today, as book nine begins: for one another.

First, the claim. Marcus opens book nine with a startling sentence: whoever acts unjustly acts impiously. A wrong done to a person is also a wrong against the order of things itself. Second, the reason. Nature, he says, made rational beings for one another, to help each other as each deserves, and never to harm. So when you harm someone, you're not just breaking a rule. You're working against what you were made for, and against the nature of the whole, which Marcus here calls the most ancient of divinities. Third, the stretch. He doesn't stop at cheating. Lying, he says, is impiety too, because the nature of the whole is truth, and the liar sets himself at odds with it, whether on purpose or carelessly. Even being thrown around by pleasure and pain, he says, ends up unjust, because it makes us unfair in how we treat people and things. Fourth, how far it reaches. Marcus's view rests on nature and the gods, and not everyone shares it. But his picture is easy to test on an ordinary day. The extra ten dollars, the excuse that wasn't true, the credit taken for someone else's work: on his view, none of them stays in its box, because the box was never separate. For Marcus we're one fabric, and a pulled thread puckers the whole cloth.

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last few days for one small wrong you did. Nothing dramatic: a sharp word, a corner cut, a promise that slid, change you didn't hand back. Don't punish yourself. Just find it. Now picture the smallest way to set it right: a message, an apology, a returned thing, a task redone. See yourself doing it. Picture the thread pulling straight. The bell holds the time.
For one another. Marcus opens book nine: nature made us to help one another, so a wrong against a person is a wrong against the whole. Today's word.
Your line: for one another. Right one small wrong today, however small. Notice how the whole feels afterward. Day six hundred six.

howItsDone: Readers who take this passage to heart often treat small wrongs as worth fixing even when no one would notice: returning the extra change, correcting the excuse, giving the credit back.

fork.setup: the cashier gives you ten dollars too much. nobody saw. you're Marcus with book nine open. what do you do?
options: keep it; the store won't notice.
hand it back: the wrong would be against the whole, not just the store.
keep it, but give the same amount away later.
fork.reveal: Marcus says injustice is impiety: we're made for one another, so even a small wrong works against the whole.

original.note: Greek: injustice, wrongdoing. book nine opens by calling it impiety.

trapdoor: what you thought: small wrongs don't really matter.
what it means: we're made for one another, so a wrong to one person is also a wrong against the whole.
what a scholar hears: Marcus calls universal nature the most ancient of divinities, so for him justice and piety become one subject.

notes: 9.1 paraphrased: injustice is impiety; nature made rational animals for one another, to help according to worth and never to harm; the transgressor is impious toward the most ancient (eldest) of divinities; the liar is impious because nature is truth (intentional and unintentional liars); being swayed by pleasure and pain leads to injustice.
